details:
**Justified true belief**
The classical definition of knowledge, usually traced to Plato's dialogue Theaetetus: knowledge is a belief that is justified and also has this property. "True" is one of the three conditions in that definition.

**Gettier problems**
Counterexamples from Edmund Gettier's 1963 paper "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" In the most famous one, a job applicant named Smith justifiably believes that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. The belief turns out true only by luck, so justified true belief does not seem to be enough for knowledge.

**Semantic theory of truth ("Snow is white")**
Alfred Tarski's theory, laid out in "The Concept of Truth in Formalized Languages." It is captured by the T-schema: "'Snow is white' is true if and only if snow is white." Tarski required a definition to be materially adequate and formally correct, treated sentences as the bearers of this property, and held that it can be defined for an object language only in a separate metalanguage.

**Truth tables**
Diagrams, popularized by Ludwig Wittgenstein in the Tractatus, that list every combination of true and false values for a statement's components. A statement with N components needs 2 to the N rows, and the tables show how logical operators such as "not," "and," and "or" determine whether a compound statement is true.

**Correspondence theory**
The view that a statement is true when it corresponds to reality, meaning to facts or states of affairs in the world. It is the most traditional theory of truth.

**Coherence theory**
The rival view that a statement is true if it is consistent with a larger system of beliefs or propositions. Coherentists reject the correspondence theory.

**Deflationary theory**
The view that saying a proposition p "is true" adds nothing to simply asserting p, so the word "true" is redundant. The redundancy theory is one version of it.

**Pragmatist theory (William James)**
Pragmatists tie truth to usefulness and practice. William James called it "the expedient in our way of thinking," and Charles Sanders Peirce saw truth as the opinion inquiry is fated to reach in the end, its ultimate goal or "end of inquiry."

**"Will to truth"**
A phrase from the opening section of Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil, which questions why philosophers value truth at all. Nietzsche suggests that this "will to truth" is itself an expression of the will to power.

**Language, Truth and Logic**
A. J. Ayer's 1936 book, the key British statement of logical positivism (logical empiricism). It holds that meaningful statements must be either analytic or empirically verifiable, and "truth" is the second of the three nouns in its title.

**Donald Davidson**
An American philosopher who built a theory of meaning on Tarski's work, holding that knowing a sentence's meaning amounts to knowing the conditions under which it would be true (its truth conditions). The "slingshot argument," which he used, claims that all true sentences refer to the same thing.

**Richard Rorty**
An American neopragmatist who argued in Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity that truths are made rather than found, since "vocabularies are made by human beings." He drew heavily on Davidson's view of truth.

**Tautologies**
Statements that are true under every possible assignment of truth values, such as "P or not P." Truth tables show this by giving "true" in every row.

**Sun analogy (Republic Book VI)**
In Book VI of Plato's Republic, the Form of the Good is compared to the sun. Just as the sun's light makes objects visible, the Good makes truth and knowledge possible for the mind.

**Consensus theory (Jürgen Habermas)**
Habermas's view that truth is what rational participants would agree on through ideal, undistorted discussion.
